      About the tracker and its method

      China–Hungary Investment Tracker is a register of investment in Hungary by mainland Chinese, Hong Kong and Macau firms and Chinese-owned foreign brands, built from the Hungarian-language press. It extends the China–Turkey Investment Tracker to Hungary, with the same unit (a project), the same evidence (one claim per article, quoted word for word and linked) and the same reading of outcomes, and it borrows the registry checks of Gürel, Selamet, Şahinli, Sen and Tuzcu (2026), Asian Perspective 50(2): 219–257. Compiled by Osman Demirbağ, Burak Gürel, Kadir Selamet. Data release 2026-10-22.

      Definitions used on the first screen

      The headline, the squares and the four further findings use these terms. Counts follow the settings chosen above the squares (currently ).

      Realised
      Operating, under construction or acquired, as last reported.
      Live promise
      Announced, agreed, in talks or rumoured, with a press report found within the last .
      Dormant promise
      No press report found for or more ( projects at 2 / 3 / 5 years). This is not a confirmed cancellation: rest on a single press report.
      Failed or exited
      A bid lost or not made (), a promise abandoned or put on hold (), or an exit after realisation, by closure or sale ().
      Promise phase
      First reported as interest, talks, a bid or a promise: of the investment projects. The promise-phase base counts only these; projects that entered the press already realised, such as completed acquisitions and sales offices, have no promise phase on record.
      Chinese
      Includes Hong Kong and Macau firms and Chinese-owned brands. Mainland firms alone: realised. Taiwanese firms are excluded.
      Not counted
      non-equity or contractor and finance items: kept in the register and the explorer, not counted as investment.

      How the register was built

      The register follows the Turkey tracker's design and adds three search stages, so that firms nobody named in advance and reports that name no firm are caught as well. Every step leaves a file in the project repository, and every number on this page is computed from those files.

      1. Stage 1, known firms. 198 Chinese, Hong Kong and Macau firms and Chinese-owned brands, plus 39 names found later, searched by name (365 spellings) in Google News (Hungarian edition) and the Index.hu archive.
      2. Stage 2, every China-related investment story. 30 Hungarian queries such as kínai beruházás, kínai befektető, hongkongi befektető or makaói, and 10 archive terms.
      3. Stage 3, registries and China's own list. The GLEIF register of legal entities (26,293 Hungarian records), and the main Chinese investors named by China's Ministry of Commerce in its country guide for Hungary.
      4. Fetch. Links resolved, pages downloaded at a polite rate, text extracted, and every sentence naming a seed firm or China next to investment vocabulary kept as a candidate.
      5. Curation. Nine curation passes turned the candidates into projects and claims, each claim with the verbatim Hungarian sentence, an English translation and the link; a script rejected any quote not found word for word in the downloaded article.
      6. Feedback. Names found in stages 2 and 3 went back into stage 1 and were searched in the same way.

      Sources

      The source list (config/sources.csv) names 75 sources: economic press (9): Portfolio, Világgazdaság, Economx, Mfor / Menedzsment Fórum, Privátbankár, Pénzcentrum, Növekedés.hu, Forbes Magyarország, Figyelő; national news with economy desks (5): HVG, Telex, Index, 24.hu, Infostart; national general news (12): 444, Híradó.hu, Magyar Nemzet, Origo, Mandiner, Népszava, Magyar Hang, Magyar Narancs, Válasz Online, RTL Híradó, ATV, Szabad Európa; news agency (1): MTI; investigative (2): Átlátszó, Direkt36; trade papers (17): Gyártástrend, Autopro, Járműipar.hu, Autó-Motor, Vezess, Totalcar, Villanyautósok, e-cars.hu, Bitport, HWSW, Computertrends, Agrárszektor, Magyar Mezőgazdaság, Trade magazin, Navigátor Világ, Magyar Építők, Energiainfo; regional dailies (16): Haon, Dehir, Debreciner, Szon, Délmagyar, Szeged.hu, Kemma, Boon, Kisalföld, Feol, Bama, Baon, Veol, Heol, Beol, Szoljon; official sources (9): Kormány.hu, HIPA, Magyar Közlöny, GVH, BÉT, EU State Aid Transparency, MNB FDI statistics, KSH, MOFCOM country guide: Hungary; registries and statistics (4): e-cegjegyzek.hu, Nemzeti Cégtár, OPTEN, GLEIF LEI data.

      Ownership of the Hungarian press matters for what gets reported. Világgazdaság, Magyar Nemzet, Origo, Mandiner and the county dailies belong to groups close to the government that was in office until 2026; HVG, Telex, 444, 24.hu, Népszava, Átlátszó and Direkt36 are independent of it. Announcements appear in both; permits, pollution, labour disputes and state-aid details mostly in the latter. The search does not depend on this list: Google News and the Index archive return any Hungarian outlet, and the claims cite 77 of them. Claims by type of outlet: national news with economy desks 277, economic press 156, other outlets 69, national general news 53, trade papers 29, regional dailies 23, investigative 22, official sources 9. Most cited: Index (162), HVG (86), Világgazdaság (79), Economx (38), 444 (30), Portfolio (28), 24.hu (20), Átlátszó (18), Dehir (13), Kormány.hu (9).

      Stage 1: known Chinese firms

      The seed list holds 198 firms in three groups: 24 already known to be in Hungary, 34 present in neighbouring countries and 140 global majors (carmakers, battery and component makers, telecom, energy, construction, banks, e-commerce). 39 names were added as the work went on: 4 from stage 3: GLEIF register; 5 from curators' archive and web searches; 24 from stage 2 news (generic queries and their curation); 6 from stage 3: China's own list (MOFCOM country guide); Zoomlion was moved up from the global list after a stage-1 find.

      Each firm was searched in Google News, Hungarian edition (hl=hu&gl=HU): by name alone over monthly windows from 2015 for firms known in Hungary (Google returns a sample, and smaller windows return more of it), over yearly windows before 2015 and for firms found later, and with Hungarian investment and place words over wide windows for the others. The Index.hu archive search, which reaches back to 1999 and covers Index's sister titles, filled the years Google News barely holds: a 2010–2012 Google query for BorsodChem returns one item, the Index archive returns the sale to Wanhua.

      Hungarian attaches case endings to names (BYD-t, CATL-nél, Huaweinél, Lenovónál); the matcher accepts a list of endings and the lengthened final vowel, so that Gree does not match Green. Names that are also Hungarian words or common surnames (KUKA is a bin, Seres a surname) were matched only in capitals and searched with context words; football clubs and unrelated companies with the same name were excluded by term.

      Stage 2: every China-related investment story

      Generic Hungarian queries catch firms that were not on the list and reports that name no firm at all (“egy kínai cég 45 milliárdot hozna …”). 30 Google News queries over yearly windows and 10 Index archive terms returned 20,354 results, of which 3,890 had China (or a seed firm) and investment vocabulary in the headline and were downloaded. Of the downloaded stage-2 articles, 569 carry a China-and-investment sentence tied to a Hungarian place; two curators read them by period (1999–2023 and 2024–2026) and scanned the headlines of the rest.

      kínai beruházáskínai befektetéskínai befektetőkínai beruházókínai cég gyárkínai cég üzemkínai vállalat Magyarországonkínai tulajdonúkínai hátterűkínai érdekeltségűkínai beszállítókínai akkumulátorgyárkínai autógyárkínai óriás magyarkínai felvásárláskínai cég megvásároltakínai munkahely milliárdegyedi kormánydöntés kínaikiemelt beruházás kínaiSzijjártó kínai beruházáskínai logisztikai központkínai napelemparkkínai bank Budapestkínai hitel beruházáshongkongi befektetőhongkongi cégmakaói befektetőkínai partner gyárkínai tulajdonos gyárkínai ipari park

      Stage 2 added 55 projects that stage 1 had not reached, among them FiberHome's optical-cable plant in Kisbér (first reported without the firm's name), Intretech in Kapuvár, Hongene's pharmaceutical plant in Gödöllő, Wescast (Bohong) in Oroszlány and the CECZ logistics park in Vác, and 56 general signals: ministerial totals, unnamed investors, delegations and policy reviews. When a report named no firm, the curators tried to identify it from the article, other articles and the registry; the Fót battery plant (BYD), the Kaposvár actuator plant (J-Star) and the Gyula pharmaceutical plant (Youcare) were identified this way.

      Stage 3: registries and China's own list

      No country list in Hungary. In Turkey, the ministry's list of foreign-capital firms gives each firm's country, and the Asian Perspective article checked it against the trade-registry gazette and the central registry. Hungary publishes no such list. The company register records each member's seat, country included, but its free interface (e-cegjegyzek.hu) searches one company at a time behind a CAPTCHA, and so does the register of annual accounts.

      GLEIF. The open register of legal entity identifiers holds 26,293 Hungarian entities with their direct and ultimate parents. Screening them listed 31: 6 with a parent in mainland China on record and 25 whose names match a seed firm or a China term. After review: 7 Chinese, 12 held by Chinese groups through other countries (LEDVANCE through Germany, COFCO through the Netherlands and the Cayman Islands, KUKA through Germany), 6 to check and 6 excluded (name matches such as ZTE Football Club). Most Chinese subsidiaries in Hungary have no identifier or report no parent, so GLEIF gives a floor, not a census.

      China's own list. China's Ministry of Commerce names, in its country guide for outward investors (对外投资合作国别（地区）指南·匈牙利, 2025 edition), the main Chinese investors in Hungary and the leading members of the Chinese chamber. Of its 32 names, 23 were on the seed list. Six were added and searched (FiberHome, Shandong Himile, Zhejiang Huashuo, Zhejiang Shuanghuan, the CECZ logistics zone, the Ganzhou land port); four of them had already surfaced in the curation, two came only from the guide. 31 of the 32 are now covered by projects; the exception, Risen Energy, only supplies solar modules.

      What the statistics say. By the end of 2024 Chinese direct investment in Hungary was USD 2.09 billion by immediate investor but USD 6.10 billion by ultimate investor (MNB data published by the OECD), and MOFCOM's own figure was USD 1.52 billion: about two thirds of Chinese-controlled capital arrives through other countries. This is the Hungarian form of the Singapore and Luxembourg problem the Asian Perspective article found in the Turkish lists, and the reason Hong Kong counts as Chinese here and holding routes are recorded (26 projects; Hong Kong 13, Germany 3, China-CEE Fund (fund vehicle) 2, Singapore 2, Netherlands 2, Switzerland 2, Luxembourg 1, British Virgin Islands 1, Canada 1).

      Downloading and reading the articles

      Google News links were resolved to the publishers' addresses and the pages downloaded at a polite rate (one request every one to two seconds per site). 9,251 articles were downloaded or logged: 7,320 from stage 1, 1,575 from stage 2 and 356 added by the curators. 8,144 came with their full text from 272 domains; 1,107 could be read only from their headline, mostly because the site refused scripted requests: telex.hu (211), totalcar.hu (134), autopro.hu (100), forbes.hu (93), magyarepitok.hu (75), notebookcheck-hu.com (71). The Internet Archive, the usual fallback for such pages, could not be reached from the environment in which the pipeline ran.

      The texts were split into 216,288 sentences. A sentence became a candidate when it named a seed firm or China (kínai, Kína, hongkongi, makaói …) next to investment vocabulary (beruházás, gyár, üzem, felvásárol, milliárd …): 28,481 sentences in 6,668 articles, 16,782 of them naming a seed firm. Each candidate carries a lifecycle tier from ordered keyword rules (failure, other, realisation, interest, promise).

      Curation: from articles to projects and claims

      A project is a firm, or an identifiable investor, tied to a site or a target in Hungary; separate sites and separately reported phases are separate projects. A claim is one article and one step: the Hungarian sentence copied character for character, its English translation, the article link, the date, the outlet and the step's label. Reports of Chinese interest that cannot be tied to a firm or site are general signals.

      The passes were merged by a script that checks every field and value and rejects a quote that does not occur word for word in the downloaded text (an ellipsis may mark an omission). 635 of the 638 claims were matched this way; 3 quote English-language reports because no Hungarian report of that step was found, 16 quote only a headline and 6 only a lead, for pages that could not be downloaded. 2 projects curated twice were folded into one, 11 field changes were made after later reports (a bid that ended without a sale, a parent documented later) and 1 project was removed; each decision is recorded with its reason. The curators logged 45 leads for follow-up.

      The English translations were written by Claude during curation, each next to its verbatim Hungarian sentence, and have not yet been reviewed by a Hungarian speaker.

      Claim types: 514 investment steps (plan, agreement, state aid, land purchase, permit, groundbreaking, opening, expansion, exit), 40 mentions in passing, 42 company news and 42 contractor or finance items. Lifecycle tiers: 197 promise, 64 interest, 138 realisation, 61 failure and 178 other.

      What was filtered out, and why

      1. At the search stage, results were kept for download only when the headline carried investment, Hungary or China vocabulary (or, for firms not known in Hungary, a Hungarian headline or the firm next to investment words): 97,638 of 107,822 results were set aside. The Index archive search stems words and returns unrelated articles for some foreign names, so its results had to name the firm in the headline or lead: Hangke Technology (27,773 results, 39 kept), Fudan University (21,203 results, 278 kept), TikTok (5,797 results, 92 kept), Livan Biodegradable (5,202 results, 13 kept), Wasion (1,893 results, 2 kept).
      2. At the reading stage, only sentences with a firm or China term next to investment vocabulary became candidates (28,481 of 216,288 sentences), and stage-2 articles had to tie such a sentence to a Hungarian place.
      3. Not Chinese. Taiwanese firms (Foxconn's plants in Komárom, Pécs and Székesfehérvár) and the Korean and Japanese battery makers (Samsung SDI, SK On, EcoPro, Toray, W-Scope) are excluded unless a Chinese firm takes part in the step; so are name matches without a Chinese link (MIDEA Kereskedőház, ZTE Football Club, TCL Media Hungary, JAC-KER). Asiafood's dumpling plant in Verpelét, reported as Chinese-owned, turned out to be French-owned and was removed; Vulcan Shield's Békéscsaba plant complex is Singapore-headquartered with no documented Chinese parent; Magnus Aircraft's “Chinese investment” is a Hungarian firm's joint venture in China.
      4. Not investment. Car brands sold through independent Hungarian importers, product launches, e-commerce parcel flows and service contracts (Temu's postal deal), and Chinese firms' plants elsewhere in Europe are not projects. Construction contracts and Chinese loans (the Budapest–Belgrade railway, state loans) are kept as contractor or finance items; airline routes, contract manufacturing for Huawei and Lenovo, licences and consortia as non-equity presence. Neither is counted as investment.
      5. Searched, but nothing in Hungary. Many names that fill the Hungarian press never invested there. Names with the most candidate articles and no project:

      • The press usually meets a project as a promise. 104 of the 148 investment projects were first reported as interest, talks or a promise; 48 of them (46%) were realised.
      • Failures: 6 bids lost or not made (European car plants of SAIC/MG and Geely, Huawei's European factory, Hangzhou CIEC's bid for the Dunarolling mill), 3 promises abandoned (KunlunChem's Szolnok electrolyte plant in 2026, RZBC's citric-acid plant, BYN's Heves plant) and 8 exits after realisation (closures in Ózd and Szombathely, sales of COFCO's Makó can plant and CMC's Kaposvár solar park).
      • Sectors: Automotive & batteries 57, Electronics, telecom & IT 29, Machinery & industry 20, Transport & logistics 12, Banking & finance 8, Agriculture & food 6. The battery and car chain (CATL, BYD, EVE, Sunwoda, Semcorp, Huayou, Kedali, Halms, Chervon …) dominates.
      • Places (investment projects): Budapest 38, Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén 24, Pest 16, Hajdú-Bihar 12, Komárom-Esztergom 9, Jász-Nagykun-Szolnok 8, Csongrád-Csanád 4, Heves 4; 19 projects name no county. Budapest is shown as one unit.
      • Timing: 83 of the 148 investment projects were first reported in 2020 or later (8 in the 2000s, 57 in the 2010s, 83 in the 2020s).
      • Origin: Mainland China 156, Chinese-owned foreign brand 9, Hong Kong 7, Origin not established 5 (all projects).
      • After the April 2026 election (89 claims and signals): the new government withdrew support for CATL's later phases, ordered a review of the Budapest–Belgrade railway contract, withdrew KunlunChem's priority status and announced a review of agreements with Chinese investors; the authorities suspended and then banned activity at Semcorp's Debrecen plant. At the same time CATL began trial production in Debrecen, Huayou/Bamo started production at Ács, and Yadea and J-Star announced new plants or halls.

      Coding choices to review

      • Sites and phases are separate projects: CATL has five (phase-1 cell plant, the leased INPARK module hall, phases 2–3, the Brunp recycling unit, the GreenPower repackaging plant); Wanhua has the BorsodChem takeover, eight plant-level investments and the LFP cathode plant.
      • Takeovers abroad (ChemChina–Syngenta, Midea–KUKA, MLS–LEDVANCE, Hisense–Gorenje, Joyson–Takata) make the Hungarian subsidiaries Chinese-owned foreign brands, with the route where documented.
      • Contract manufacturing for Huawei and Lenovo is non-equity presence; the DHL-run Huawei logistics centre in Biatorbágy is a Huawei facility.
      • Builder and owner: the Kaposvár solar park was built and owned by CMC (Genertec) through Hong Kong and British Virgin Islands holders and sold to MVM in 2023, so it is an exit, not a contractor job.
      • Stoppages: a plant stopped by the authorities stays realised, with the stoppage as a claim (Semcorp, 2025–2026).
      • Origin not established for 5 projects whose owners are described only as Chinese investors or a Chinese family, where diaspora ownership cannot be excluded.

      Stages, outcomes, figures and the map

      Stages and outcomes

      Each project carries the stage it reached as last reported: realised or under way, agreed or announced, interest, talks or a bid, rumour, failed, lost or exited, non-equity presence, and contractor or finance only. The site reads the stage together with the time since the last report, as the Turkey tracker does. Realised and failed follow the stage. Announced, agreed, in-talks or rumoured projects are live promises while a report falls inside the dormancy window and dormant promises once none has been found for that long (three years by default; two and five are offered). A dormant promise means that no evidence of progress was found, not that the project was cancelled. A non-equity arrangement or a contract or loan is never counted as investment, even when its stage records that it ended (the Fudan campus, contract manufacturing).

      Claims and lifecycle tiers

      Each claim has a lifecycle tier read from its event label with ordered rules: failure words first, then later references and denials as “other”, then realisation, commitment and interest. The first realisation-tier claim dates a realisation, the first failure-tier claim a failure, and the first claim's tier records how the press first found the project. The time-to-outcome chart estimates the cumulative incidence of realisation and failure for projects first reported as interest or a promise (Aalen–Johansen), treating projects still open at the release as censored.

      Reported figures

      96 projects report a headline figure. Each was read by hand and classed by what it measures: 71 pledge, 11 contract finance, 6 parent deal, 3 registered capital, 2 project cost, 1 invested, 1 unparsed, 1 elsewhere. Only announced pledges are compared across outcomes (71 projects). Most Hungarian figures are in forint or euro; they are converted to US dollars at the ECB annual average rate of the year the figure was reported (the current year at the average of the months published), so that they sit on the Turkey tracker's scale. Where the press reports a larger sum invested after an announcement (Semcorp), the announcement is used so that promises are compared with promises. Figures are as announced and not verified.

      The map

      Counties are those named in the articles, with Budapest as one unit; a project with sites in several counties is counted in each, and 19 projects with no reported county are listed under “No county reported”. Outlines: Eurostat GISCO, NUTS 2021 level 3 (© EuroGeographics for the administrative boundaries), with the neighbouring countries for orientation and Lake Balaton from Natural Earth; Lambert conformal conic projection with standard parallels at 46°N and 48°N.

      The first screen and the explorer

      The headline, the squares and the four further findings describe all investment projects as last reported, on the comparison base and dormancy threshold chosen there; explorer filters do not change them, they highlight the matching projects. Outcome, sector, origin and form filters are inclusive within a group and combine across groups. A link to any view can be copied from the results bar, and each project opens its evidence timeline with the Hungarian quotes, their translations and links to the articles.

      Limits

      This is a register of press reports, not of capital flows. A promise can be realised without the press noticing, and a realised project may have had a promise phase no archive captured. Google News holds only a sample of Hungarian news, thin before 2015; the Index archive and targeted searches fill part of the gap. Telex refused scripted requests throughout the run and the Internet Archive could not be reached, so some steps rest on other outlets or on a headline. Owners and registration numbers of several Hungarian subsidiaries still need a check of the official company extract; they are listed in the curation notes of each project. Recent cohorts are right-censored, and some associations are built into the data: holding routes are documented mostly once a company exists, and a named county is itself a sign of progress. Treat such differences as descriptive.
